text: QAOA, the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm, is the circuit that actually runs the Ising Hamiltonians you built in Chapter 1 on quantum hardware. This lesson lays out its skeleton -- what gates fire, in what order, and why the circuit has exactly 2p tunable numbers for a depth-p circuit.

Every QAOA circuit has the same three-part shape. State preparation applies a Hadamard to every qubit, producing an equal superposition over all 2 to the n candidate bitstrings. Then p alternating layers each apply a cost unitary built from the problem's cost Hamiltonian, followed by a mixer unitary built from a fixed mixer Hamiltonian. Finally, measurement reads out bitstrings repeatedly, and you keep the best one seen. Each layer contributes exactly two parameters, gamma and beta, so a depth-p circuit has exactly 2p tunable parameters total.

Running an exact state-vector simulation of a depth-1, 2-qubit circuit on a single-edge Max-Cut problem: at gamma equals pi over 2 and beta equals pi over 8, the circuit never measures an uncut assignment -- it lands on one of the two cut assignments with 100% combined probability, an expected cost of exactly 1.0, the true maximum. At poorly chosen angles, gamma equals 0.1 and beta equals 0.1, the same circuit's expected cost drops to only about 0.519 -- worse than a coin flip's worth of signal. Same circuit, same problem, wildly different quality.

QAOA is called 'variational' because, while the circuit's gate structure is fixed in advance, the 2p numerical parameters inside it are not -- they're adjusted iteratively by a classical optimizer running outside the quantum computer, using measured expectation values as feedback. This hybrid loop, where the quantum circuit evaluates a candidate and the classical optimizer proposes the next one, is the defining pattern of every algorithm in this course, VQE included. The quantum hardware never learns; it only ever evaluates.

Next lesson writes H_C and H_B out explicitly as sums of Pauli operators, so you can see exactly why the mixer is almost always built from Pauli-X, and why the two unitaries can't simply be merged into one.
